utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. I ask that the next witness be kept out of court for the moment to deal with two issues. Mr. Tieger, thank you for your estimate of the time that you will need. It seems, accordingly, that it's unlikely that we're going to get through all the witnesses that are scheduled before the planned adjournment. Does the OTP have a view on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Our biggest concern, as the Court is aware, has been the fixed witnesses. I think we will manage that, but I agree, we will have to take on board the adjustment in schedule for other witnesses, and we're looking at that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's the best thing. And, Mr. Robinson, I don't ask for any particular response, but obviously the position of the Defence in respect of that will have to be taken into account. It was the Chamber that asked for this witness to be -- or the previous witness to be viva voce, and that has led to the extension of time, so if there are any corresponding difficulties for the Defence, no doubt you will raise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The other thing is this, that Dr. Karadzic has filed his motion for the fifth suspension of proceedings. It would be very useful if the Prosecution could provide an expedited response to that before the beginning of next week, i.e., before Monday, the 14th of March. Even if that response is not as full as it otherwise might have been, at least to set out the essence of the case. Obviously again for forward planning purposes. Thank you very much. Now the witness can come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If we could just return to a matter that you raised yesterday concerning General Smith's private and public session. I was discussing this with Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I'm sorry, Mr. Robinson. I think this is going to raise matters that should be addressed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We're back to the timing schedule we've been following to date today, so we'll take a break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, are we sitting until 1.45 or 2.30 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's 1.45, I'm sure. Yes. Yes, 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare -- I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If you'd like to sit down and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Witness, as you will have observed, the curtains have now raised, but you cannot be seen from the public gallery, and indeed you cannot be seen in the -- on the video because of the image distortion, and I simply caution you when you are giving your answers not to say anything that might reveal your identity. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we begin, please, by calling up 65 ter 90238, and of course that's not to be broadcast. And before I move on to this document, Your Honour, perhaps in accordance with previous practice, I could recognise the presence of and introduce to the Court certain officials who are here today and who are seated at the portion of the room to the left of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, you see before you 65 ter 90238. Do you recognise that as an amalgamated witness statement comprising information and evidence that you have previously provided to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This is my amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review that statement, and does it accurately reflect the information you previously provided and was that information truthful and accurate to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I had the opportunity to review this document several times, and it is word-for-word the previous statements that I gave to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if asked about the same matters here in court, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I would not change anything in what I have stated previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in accordance with 92 ter I would tender 90238 for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. As Exhibit P2414, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I don't know when the Trial Chamber wishes to address the associated exhibits, but there is one matter I would raise in connection with that, and that would be that with respect to the 65 -- the fifth item listed on the exhibits referenced in the statement that's dated 1 August 1995, which is a newspaper article referenced during the course of earlier information, although we initially indicated that we would not tender that for admission, largely because of the guidelines referring to newspaper articles, we took another look at that and thought that the nature of the discussion and basically in fairness to the Defence under these circumstances it could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We welcome the admission of that document and we don't object to the admission of any of the other associated documents with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then they will all be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with the Court's leave, I would read a brief summary of the -- a very brief summary of the amalgamated statement. Witness KDZ182 served with UNPROFOR in Sarajevo in late 1994 and 1995. The witness provided -- provides evidence that for large periods of time, Sarajevo was unable to function properly due to restrictions on access for humanitarian convoys and shelling and sniping attacks directed at its inhabitants perpetrated by Bosnian Serb forces. Sniping incidents against civilians and UNPROFOR personnel were investigated by UNPROFOR personnel. They concluded that the vast majority of sniping incidents in and around Sarajevo were perpetrated by Bosnian Serb forces. UNPROFOR anti-sniping measures aimed at protecting the civilian population were directed almost exclusively at Serb snipers. Protests about attacks on civilians were made by UNPROFOR to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and in particular letters of protest were sent to the commander, Dragomir Milosevic. Milosevic would either claim that the Muslims fired first or would simply not respond. The treatment of UN personnel taken hostage in May 1995 was also protested directly to the corps commander. From his own observations and according to information received by the witness, General Ratko Mladic controlled the strategy in Sarajevo while it was Dragomir Milosevic's job to implement this vision. Colonel Indic, a liaison officer at Lukavica, acted as Mladic's eyes and exerted pressure on Milosevic to ensure Mladic's vision was carried out. That concludes the summary, Your Honour, and with the Court's permission, I would ask the witness a number, a limited number, of additional questions. And if we could move first into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to ask you about a number of different areas. Let me begin with this one: At page 28 of your statement, and I believe in other portions as well, and I think that's both in the French and English version, you refer to weapons collection points, and I wanted to ask you, although I think there's some reference to that in your statement, whether those weapons collection points were, in fact, points. That is, were they small contained areas like a box or a single storage facility or were they something else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes. This admittedly is a topic which was subject of concern at the time I was there. Even if the arms collection point on the Bosnian side were areas which could be controlled entirely by UNPROFOR, the arms collection points on the Serbian side were not closed or easily identified locations. The arms, whether they be barrels or mortars, were largely placed in the field, and UNPROFOR soldiers were unable to control these on a permanent basis and did not know when these weapons were used, because these collection points were very close to the areas where the Serbian soldiers lived. As I stated in my statement, the only possibility we had, more often than not, was to check the hot barrel theory. Unfortunately, the Serbs used these weapons to shoot. Since we were far removed from these

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we move into private session quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is almost a bizarrely unhelpful intervention once we've moved back into open session particularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we now move into private session to address this and redact that portion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, at page 41 of your amalgamated statement, in both the English and French versions, there is a discussion during which you were asked about how frequently or how regularly civilians were the target of Serb snipers, and you said that you could not give a precise answer but indicated that 66 fires from snipers in the Serb sector were identified, and also indicated that there were six incidents from the Bosnian sector into Serb-held territory, although in those cases UNPROFOR -- UNPROFOR was unable to verify the Serb claim that those were civilian victims because there were not UNPROFOR soldiers posted in that area to confirm. And, Witness, my question is: Were those identified snipings, did they represent all of the sniping incidents during the period of time you were there or just a portion, and if the latter, can you indicate the difference?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: The identified sniping you're talking about here are only a minor quantity of the total amount of sniping incidents in Sarajevo. Why? Because given the curve of the confrontation line and given the lack of presence in certain areas of United Nations observers or United Nations soldiers, we could only count the sniping incidents which we knew the origin of. Therefore, the figures provided here are only a negligible amount of the total fires targeted at the population in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although the other incidents to which you referred were not identified to UNPROFOR's satisfaction to the extent of those 72 incidents, that is the 66 versus 6, did you receive enough information about them either individually or collectively to be able to say which faction was responsible for the bulk of those incidents, or whether they were equally distributed, or whether you didn't get sufficient information at all?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: When I say 66 versus 6, I'm talking about firing incidents, the origin of which was established, verified. For the rest, there was a lot of firing, but since we were not able to identify them, we did not mention them in our reports. However, the general impression of the people on the ground was that there was no equal distribution between the firing incidents. The proportion of shootings coming from the Serb faction seemed to be much higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, let me ask you a couple of questions about shelling attacks on the city's population by Bosnian Serb forces. You refer in a number of portions of your amalgamated statement to the strategy of shelling and sniping of the civilian population by the Bosnian Serb forces. Let me ask you first whether you were aware of the presence of military objects such as headquarters within the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I knew where the Bosnian corps was located in the city of Sarajevo, the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when UNPROFOR forces considered, investigated, reviewed, or assessed shelling of the city, did they consider the presence of either the main headquarters or other headquarters or military -- other military objects in determining what the object of the shelling had been?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR soldiers did not have access to the staff, the Main Staff, of the Bosnian corps, and when there was shelling, the only places where we would go to were areas within the city, but we never had access to Bosnian military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me -- I understood, and I understood that it was a confusing question. Let me ask the question in this way: Bearing in mind the presence of military headquarters or other military objects in the city, can you tell the Court about the nature of the shelling of the city that took place that led you to understand that it was the population that was being targeted?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the desire of the Serbs to reach Bosnian military targets in particular, but what I know is that the corps command and maybe other installations as well were in the city itself and were, therefore, collateral, so to speak, to the population. And even if the Bosnian military targets were targeted, it -- of course, so was the population, and the population was submitted to many shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of shelling of the city -- were you aware of shelling of purely residential areas, for example?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Of course. It is obvious there were areas which to my knowledge and to the knowledge of UNPROFOR as a whole there was no military target, those shellings aimed at the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to areas of the city that were shelled, areas where there were military, some or one or any military objects, what was it about the nature of the shelling that indicated to you that the population was being submitted to shelling as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: The impression that UNPROFOR people had is that not only military objectives were targeted, but that more generally the overall strategy of Serb forces was to shell the population as well and to create a climate of fear and terror within the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in areas where there were -- where there was a military object or military objects, were shells concentrated on that particular object or were they dispersed around the entire area? Including where civilians were.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I never had the feeling that those shellings focused exclusively on military targets. The shellings were dispersed, and civilians were also taken as targets. I don't think it was selective shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, let me begin again, because I think that this could be in open session. You refer in your amalgamated statement to the anti-sniping agreement and the reduction in people wounded and killed in Sniper Alley, and indicate that was a demonstration of the control that the factions had over the snipers. You also indicated earlier in your statement and at the same page that protests to General Milosevic sometimes -- that the -- as a result, the frequency of the sniping incidents diminished, didn't cease but would diminish for a period. Was that another factor signalling control over snipers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Snipers who were on the ground for the Serb faction created a lot of problem, and after a while an anti-sniping mechanism, so to speak, was established by UNPROFOR in order to inform the snipers, the Serb snipers, that if they were to shoot, they might be neutralised by UNPROFOR shooters. Like I said, this mechanism reduced the activity of those snipers. Those snipers were Serb shooters who were part of a military organisation, and they shot according to the orders that they'd received. In my opinion, the orders were that they should use any opportunity to target the population and later on to target UNPROFOR soldiers. Therefore, I believe that those shooters were part of an overall strategy -- or, rather, within an overall tactics defined by General Milosevic, and they had some freedom to target any available targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. At a number of points in your amalgamated statement you make the point that it was General Mladic who was the strategist and General Milosevic the technician in Sarajevo. That's contained, for example, at page 16 of your amalgamated statement, and you continue that General Mladic elaborated a general strategy, a strategy of terror, and General Milosevic would execute it within the general strategy and that his -- and then you also mention Colonel Indic, who would be General Mladic's eyes to ensure that the actions taken in Sarajevo were consistent with the general strategy. I won't outline all the points in your statement where you discuss this, but I would ask you if you could identify for the Court some of the factors that brought you to this understanding of the distinction between the global strategy of General Mladic and the execution of that strategy by General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: After a certain amount of months on the ground, and I realised that there was an overall strategic concept which had been defined by General Mladic and that the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, General Milosevic, was using what he thought were appropriate means to carry out the strategy. The strategist was Milosevic and the tactician -- I'm sorry, the strategist was Mladic and the technician was Milosevic. I give an example, a specific example, in my amalgamated statement. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: It was a very clear example of the role attributed to these various people, a good example of their attitude and reactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if -- if we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, at several portions of your amalgamated statement you indicate the nature of the hierarchy of planning and controlling operations. For example, at page 11 of the English, and I believe page 11 of the French as well, you state that these operations were planned and carried out by Bosnian Serbs at the highest level. At page 13, you say -- that's again of the English and the French, that it's your view that all the incidents in Sarajevo were orchestrated, guided, and designed by General Mladic, which is why he had Milosevic controlled by Indic. I'd like to show you a couple of documents that I don't believe you've -- I have no reason to think you've seen before. The first is 65 ter 21880. I'd like you -- what we have for 65 ter 21880 is both in English and a B/C/S version. I don't know the extent of your English reading comprehension skills, so let me read out -- tell you what that document is and read out particular portions of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could also have the English on the screen, please. No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We don't have the English uploaded as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you to all the technical wizards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, you can see both the English and B/C/S, and if at some point it's helpful, we can enlarge any portion of that at your request. This is a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 6 November 1994, and it's -- has the time of 0100 hours. It says "Very urgent. To deliver immediately to President of Republika Srpska for information to the SRK command, the 3rd Sarajevo command, the Ilidza PBR command, and the 2nd Sarajevo PBR command." And as we -- in the preamble it refers to information received concerning a meeting of local authorities and the adoption of decisions by them, and then on the next page we see an order. And if we could turn the page of the English. And as you can see from the bottom of the page, Witness, that order is from General Mladic, and it says the following: "I forbid all activities aimed at the blockade of UNPROFOR and the seizure of heavy weapons under their control without my specific order and approval. "2. I forbid the planning and carrying out of any offensive combat operation without the approval of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army or the implementation of operations planned without the agreement and approval of the Main Staff. "3. I forbid firing from large calibre weapons at civilian targets in Sarajevo without my approval." And if we could turn quickly to 65 ter 11401. And this document, Mr. Witness, is a document of the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade, which was mentioned in the earlier order as being a recipient of the Mladic order, and it says at the top: "We have received a telegram from the VRS Main Staff, which we copy here completely, as follows." And then it provides the same order you saw previously, including the forbidding of activities related to UNPROFOR, the planning of offensive activities, and the forbidding of weapons of heavy calibre on civilian targets in Sarajevo "without my approval," and it's the one signed by General Mladic. Witness, I had earlier directed your attention to portion -- those portions of your statement where you indicate that events, incidents in Sarajevo were orchestrated and designed by General Mladic. Do these documents change your view in any way, or are they consistent with your view as expressed in the amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: These two documents, which I'm seeing for the first time, corroborate the view I had initially and are tangible proof of the fact that the global strategy in Sarajevo was indeed designed, controlled, and supervised by General Mladic. In my view, this simply confirms what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender these documents for admission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P2419 and 2420, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, it's now Dr. Karadzic's opportunity to cross-examine. Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning. Good morning, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. As for my earlier intervention, I apologise once again, because I thought we were in private session. Witness, sir, do you know that this meeting was held and that this information that General Mladic referred to was correct? I'm referring to the last document we looked at.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I see this document for the first time, and I did not know and I could not know that such a meeting had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this document, did you encounter any other document or information that would confirm that the meeting was held and that this decision by the civilian authority of the Sarajevo municipality was adopted? In the follow-up events, did anything confirm that representatives of the Sarajevo municipalities adopted this decision?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what "representatives of the Sarajevo municipalities" mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I am going to draw your attention to this: I have an information that on the 5th of November, 1994, a meeting took place between the local Serb leaders of the Serbian Sarajevo in Vogosca. Serbian Sarajevo meaning the Sarajevo municipalities at which the commander and so on and so forth was present. Did you come across any document indicating that this meeting was actually held and that this decision was actually adopted, or is this the only trace of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. I don't remember having seen any other documents. I would, however, like to ask for clarification. Do you talk about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps when you talk about the Serbian municipalities, or are you talking about another entity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Witness, sir, the introduction is the most important thing. General Mladic had heard that the civilian authorities were interfering in military issues, so he heard, he has information and is warning the military structures that they should not do that. I'm asking you something else, though. Were you informed about the tensions between the civilian authorities and the Serbian Army during that period?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: All right. I had no knowledge whatsoever, had no information whatsoever of any tension or no tension between the civilian authorities and the military authorities. This was not part of my thought process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree, Witness, that each side is also responsible for its own civilians, meaning that it cannot conduct its combat actions from an inhabited area, civilian area and in that way expose the population to enemy fire. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: It is quite clear that the civilian populations must not be used as targets. I use this term deliberately, and the Geneva Conventions prohibit this. The civilian population should not be caught up in a military conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So would you agree that neither the Muslim side would be allowed to violate Resolutions of the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I would answer your question and say that the number of shelling and action against the civilian population, the Muslim population, could in no way be compared with shelling against the Serbian population. The aggression from the Serb forces against the Muslim population was much greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to answer with a yes or a no. We will come to what you would like to say against the Serbs, but let's look at this now. Would you agree that the Muslim side should not violate Resolutions of the Security Council? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Neither party must breach this rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the ban on the misuse of the exclusion zone and violations of the security of the safe area would also refer to the -- or apply to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: In the exclusion -- in the 20-kilometre exclusion zone, the UNPROFOR forces controlled the area where the Bosnian forces were located more specifically, and as far as I know, there were only very few mishaps on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you that, Witness, sir. What I'm asking you is this: Does any norm or ban apply equally to each side? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Of course. This concerned all parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Muslim side then also -- is it not supposed to cause unnecessary difficulties and suffering to civilians by acting in the same zones?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I have said already. Neither party was entitled to nor could create difficulties for the population, whichever it may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that neither side is permitted to attack the exclusion zone or the safe area and that neither side can launch an initiative from the exclusion zone or the safe zone? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: As far as demilitarised zone is concerned, the DMZ more specifically, I would like to specify that some actions were undertaken to make sure that the Bosnians in that area would leave, and these were actions undertaken by UNPROFOR soldiers which corroborated the totally impartial position of UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... come to the demilitarised zones. We will come to that. We are talking about Sarajevo now as an exclusion zone, total exclusion zone, as a zone that should be treated as a safe area even though it wasn't. So this is the formulation which should have been treated as a safe area. Can you please tell us if you know who General Nikolai is? You don't have to refer to your own relationship.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes, I knew this general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3377, please. 1D3377.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think this could be broadcast, Your Excellencies. Are there any limitations to broadcasting this? Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: One moment, Dr. Karadzic. Let me just -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any restrictions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, it can be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This general is writing to General Rasim Delic on the 26th of April, 1995, about violations of heavy weapon violations of safe areas, exclusion zones. And it says here that over the last two months, an increasing number of these violations has occurred as recorded by the UNPROFOR: "[In English] These reports have all been confirmed through several independent sources which makes me convinced that you do not observe the relevant Security Council Resolutions." [Interpretation] And then a bit lower: "[In English] You have also been warned that the abuse of principles of safe areas in this way may cause unacceptable and great risks for the civilian population in these areas." [Interpretation] And somewhat lower: "[In English] Therefore I demand that all heavy weapons within the exclusion zone be returned to the weapon collection points and that safe areas should not be abused by launching military operations from them. [Interpretation] Did you know about this? Was this letter sent to General Delic without any foundation or grounds, or were there any grounds for such a strict letter?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: This letter was written by General Nikolai, as you indicated yourself. As regards Sarajevo, we were not made aware of the fact that weapons which were collected in the Bosnian weapons collection points had been extracted and used. However, many weapons from the Serb collection points were used -- extracted first by the Serbs and then used for other areas, other exclusion zones or for the other safe areas, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we'll take a break now until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I understand there's a point you wish to raise, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the sake of the truth and for the record, I have to say this: This witness had conducted dozens of interviews with various people, with various offices of the Prosecution, and the product of that is his amalgamated witness [as interpreted] which contains 95 pages of everything that this witness had stated. However, this statement is full of generalisation, general impressions, and general feelings. It has a weight of an average indictment, and it is absolutely sufficient for someone to be convicted on the basis of this unless everything is clarified. Whatever this witness said to the detriment of both the Serbs and myself is something that we can disprove through documents. I have been given five hours to cross-examine this witness. Five days wouldn't be enough, though, because this is a huge amount of material. It's very specific, it's very arbitrary, and very dangerous. Please take this into consideration, and let's find a way for the Defence to be given an opportunity to discuss and shed light on every point which is detrimental to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I take it that what you're actually doing is asking for more than five hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Ninety-five pages, a huge number of statements that are incorrect, and we have proof of that. Whatever we have not enough time to deal with will remain as a danger for conviction to be rendered. If the Defence is not given an opportunity to disprove and dispute this, then how are we going to have a fair trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, continue at the moment, Dr. Karadzic, and the Chamber will consider whether or not to grant you more time in due course. You will understand that the time allocation which is given takes into account the assessment of the witness's evidence as the Chamber sees it, and you can rest assured that if the Chamber takes the view that there are material matters that you need to deal with, then time is given for those. If the Chamber takes the view that there are material matters -- that the matters are immaterial, those are matters that you should by definition not be too concerned about, but let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know the Court doesn't -- and I understand how the Court handled it, but I'd like to make just a couple of quick points. First of all, some of the material includes cross-examination that took place, so very unfair to characterise it in that way. Secondly, this is a repetition of what we've seen before during which in the guise of requesting additional time the accused uses that opportunity as a basis for broad-based claims, accusations, allegations, commentary that's not appropriate, and we should continue to keep an eye on it. I understand the Court's view in light of the fact that these kinds of requests have been made before followed by cross-examination which is focused on any number of peripheral issues rather than allegedly central issues, this -- the Court's intention to follow the cross-examination and make any decision on this request on the basis of a concrete scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, of course that's the essence of the trial, Mr. Tieger, but there isn't unlimited time with the best will in the world, and all parties, and particularly the Defence in cross-examination, need to be particularly astute, to focus on those matters which are actually indicted rather than broader-based material that doesn't go to the core of the indictment. Dr. Karadzic knows the position, and you can be assured that the Judges do. Let's have the witness back in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I am sorry for the delay, Mr. Witness. Dr. Karadzic, when the curtains have been raised, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you are therefore ascertaining that this letter from General Nikolai was drafted not on the basis of the developments in Sarajevo but elsewhere; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: It is not up to me to make a value judgement on a letter drafted by General Nikolai. I don't know was -- what his state of mind was and what information he had to write this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that depending on one's mood, such serious warnings are issued by a certain person? As I read it, there is a general who is warning another general that Geneva Conventions and other international covenants were in breach. How can you say that that depends on one's particular state of mind and mood?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Maybe this wasn't the right word, or maybe it wasn't translated appropriately. I don't know what information was at General Nikolai's disposal when he wrote this letter, so I do not have any value judgement on this letter, positive or negative, because I wasn't there when he wrote this letter, and he did not talk to me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of April, 1995, I believe falls within the context of this cross-examination. The phrase "state of mind" was translated for me as "mood." This is why I asked you this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Our position, Mr. Witness, which we are going to prove by a series of documents, is that the Serbian side had no interest or reason or intention whatsoever to launch any operations in Sarajevo. All our operations in Sarajevo were responses to the provocations and attacks by the Muslims. From your responses given in the amalgamated statement and in examination-in-chief, one may deduce that it was the Serbs who initiated all the attacks on Sarajevo. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is my position. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Dr. Karadzic, the last exchange is an absolutely concise example of what I meant. The first from lines 22, to 36, 1, was totally unnecessary. So half your time was spent on making a statement. If you extrapolate that into the whole of your cross-examination, and you've wasted time accordingly, that would be 2.5 out of the 5 hours gone. All you needed to do was say what you said in lines 2, 3, and 4 of 36. That's an exact example of the waste of time that both I and other Judges have talked about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I appreciate this, Your Excellency, but in order not to refer to each and every paragraph where the witness stated this, I wanted to hear from him that that was his general view about the Serbs' conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, look at this document. In your statement, Mr. Witness, you said that there were two periods of intensive deterioration of the situation. That's page 27 of your amalgamated statement in which you cited these two periods of extremely worsening military situation in Sarajevo, that is in November and October of 1994 and May to June 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now look at this UN document dated the 21st of May. Go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a very minor clarification. I think that portion of the statement refers to November/December 1994, and April/May 1995, rather than very minor -- rather than October/November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness confirmed that there were periods in which the number of incidents increased. I'm going to read it. It's page 27 of his consolidated statement. It reads: "[In English] When I first arrived, the frequency or, rather, the intensity of the incidents was fairly weak, but it increased very quickly. As of late October, nearly November, it slowed down a bit over the winter but stepped up again quite intensively as of April, May, 1995." [Interpretation] And so on. "[In English] So there are two major peaks during my tenure there, November/December, and April/May."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let's look at this page. We shall disregard paragraph 2 where the Serbs are sending conciliatory messages. Let's look at this portion: "[In English] Heavy fighting erupts in Sarajevo. Sarajevo was engulfed in heavy fighting on 16th and 17th May. More than 1.500 detonations were recorded around the city on May 16 and more than 1.200 on 17th of May. The daily average until two weeks ago was less than 20. The fighting erupted in the morning of 16th of May when Bosnian forces fired several mortar rounds at the main Serbian military base in Lukavica, a suburb south-west of Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Is this a UN document that confirms that on the 16th and 17th of May, the Muslim forces initiated the fighting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: In this document, as far as I can remember, it doesn't say that they initiated the fighting. The document says they fired, but it does not specify who had started firing. What I can say is that I was in the Debelo Brdo area, and I can say that many incidents were initiated by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Witness, the Defence cannot accept so many general statements of yours. It says here: "[In English] The fighting erupted in the morning of 16th of May when Bosnian forces fired several mortars." [Interpretation] Do you mean to say that it wasn't them who started it and that it is not demonstrated in this document? "[In English] Shortly after that, the Serbs began to concentrate bombardment of Bosnian positions on Debelo Brdo and elsewhere." [Interpretation] If you're not going to take this document into account, Mr. Witness, what are we to do? It seems that you are really minded to accused the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: My intention is not to accused either party. What I mean, and I indicated it in my statement, is that there was a peak in the shelling, a strong peak, and in my statement I do not indicate specifically who was shelling. I just indicated that there was firing, and this document, this document which I did not draft, provides information that I am not in a position to verify or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Most probably since I was one of the recipients, but I do not have a clear memory today of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 2 reads: "[In English] It seems the Serbs who were on the attack on 16th of May were trying to push the Bosnians off the Debelo Brdo high ground." [Interpretation] Is this what is written here and were you at Debelo Brdo where the Serbs were trying to drive the Muslims away?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the intensity of the fighting there, I went to see for myself what was going on. I was there at dawn on the 17th, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, as far as the admission of the document, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, no.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3364. MR. KARADZIC [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the first shells at Lukavica, at the barracks in Lukavica, could it have been the case that you missed them and that you actually didn't know who started the fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: As I indicated in my testimony, the UNPROFOR forces counted specifically all the incidents of which they knew the origin. When we did not manage to know who had started it, we did not give any indication as to the origin of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I direct your attention now to a report of the Secret Service of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian portion thereof, from mid-May. Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Defence, Security And Information Service. Now, let's look at the first sentence which reads that: "The attack was carried out on 16th of May at 9.00 by the BH Army who fired two shells from the barrack of Bistrik towards Grbavica and at the same time from the barrack prison of Ramiz Salcin, formerly Victor Bubanj, towards Lukavica. The VRS fired back, and afterwards, a general attack of the BH Army started on two axes." End of quote. Do you agree that Grbavica is a Serbian civilian residential area in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I knew Lukavica. The part I knew was where Serb units were located. I never actually went to the area where the population lived. I went to meetings held in Lukavica in the military area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you will agree about Grbavica, that that was a civilian neighbourhood close to Holiday Inn; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Are you talking about Grbavica? Indeed, Grbavica was a residential area where the population lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at what follows: "At the same time political activities were undertaken in order to involve the UN into the conflict and to provoke the activities of NATO aircraft, accusing the Serbs for starting the conflict and that they are opening fire against the civilian targets. In regards to the aforementioned, commander of the UNPROFOR Sarajevo Sector, at a meeting at 1605 with Prime Minister Silajdzic, accused the BH side for starting the activities that were carried out from the populated areas and the vicinity of the UN establishments in the town in order to attract the Serbian artillery as well as that UN would -- will not be involved in the conflict. It shall do so only in case of being under attack." Did you have information about this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: When this document says so, it means that UNPROFOR soldiers were able to assess the origin of the initial firing, and the person in charge of that area was only saying who had fired. For the rest, I don't think it was up to him. Things had to be done at a different level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "It is interesting that immediately after that statement, fire was opened at the observation point of the United Nations above the Jewish Cemetery and an APC of the UN with a Russian crew." And then lower it says: "Fire is being opened from RTV Sarajevo where the UN is located, and close to the Main Staff of the UN in Djura Djakovica Street, and from the former student facility on Bjelave above the Kosevo hospital, garage of MUP located next to the embassy, barracks on Bistrik," et cetera, et cetera. Can you see the other side is informing its leadership with a -- by a secret document about what is happening in Sarajevo and that completely proves that the Muslim side was initiating and carrying out war tricks in order to accuse the Serbs and to bring the United Nations into the conflict?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I believe that this document illustrates this ambiguity. Some events were indeed initiated by the Bosnians. We need to remain reasonable about this. But given the position of the UN forces, the quasi-majority of incidents, even if some of these incidents originated from the Bosnian side, most of them were initiated by the Serbs. So this document specifies a fact, and this is on a one-off basis. To my mind, this does not reflect a general attitude. This is how I interpret this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence will prove that it's the other way round, that -- that there were only a few incidents from the Serbian side. So we would now like to try to specify or to connect each of your general statements to specify incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the next page, please. I think it's the same page for the English and the Serbian documents. It states: "It is our estimation that the purpose of the activities carried out from the town was to provoke the VRS in order for them to open fire against the UN and civil targets as well as to justify the future action of lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo in front of the international public. "On the same day, the UN initiated negotiations between the parties Hajrulahovic-Tolimir at Sarajevo airport. A cease-fire was arranged which was not complied with because in the morning of the 17th of May at 0900 hours, the sides mutually opened fire again from the positions the Armija. "In the evening hours an offer from Nikola Koljevic was announced in which he offered a cease-fire, opening of the airport," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that document of the UN also talks about this conciliatory offer from Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I remember the discussions. Koljevic did indeed say that it would be desirable for the level of violence to come down, and he explained and made proposals which we discussed, as I remember. I believe this was a demonstration of the goodwill on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1119, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, during the war did you have access to internal documents of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps orders, directives, and so on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: No. I had no documents coming from the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you didn't even know precisely what the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps' area of responsibility was, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that calls -- I ask for a redaction at lines 17 through 20, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. That's necessary, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the amalgamated statement. This is 2414, page 26. Or I can read it. Yes, really, we're losing too much time. If all the sides have the page I can read it. "[In English] I knew that he had an area of responsibility that encompassed Sarajevo. I did not know exactly what was the scope of the area of responsibility that had been entrusted to him." [Interpretation] Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: That is indeed my answer. This is why I tried to discuss matters with him, to get an understanding of the area in question, because I never quite understood what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't have joint documents. You didn't know what the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of responsibility was, so on the basis of sense, you came out with an assessment of what the strategic intentions were of the Serbian Army and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in relation to the area of Sarajevo. Based on feelings and beliefs. That was not translated properly. So you reached far-reaching conclusions and made different statements saying that you knew what the Serb intentions were, what the Serbian strategic concept was in relation to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: These were not assumptions. I might ask to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to broadcast. Can I ask the parties to look at page 54 of the amalgamated statement, in the middle. I am not going to begin from the beginning. "[In English] ... Did you either observe or receive the information regarding the existence or otherwise of co-ordination between SRK units who were engaged in attacking the civilian population?" [Interpretation] The answer is: "[In English] I haven't had such information. I only had a feeling and an impression."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is confusing me, Witness, sir, is your readiness to believe. And belief actually depends completely on our willingness to believe something or not. However, the Defence must show what you knew without any reasonable doubt, and we need to get that and not conclusions, actually not your feelings or impressions. Please look at what you said on page 24 at the top. Question was: "[In English] With regard to your view of Milosevic, you believed that Milosevic was a straw man; correct?" Not "strange," "straw." "I had the feeling that he didn't control the whole situation." [Interpretation] And we are dealing with an impression of yours; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I wish to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure that my next question should be in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's why -- my question was misinterpreted as a direction. That's why I prefaced it with "can we." It should have been "may we." Very well. Let's go back into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I trust that the reason for my being on my feet is clear. I would ask for redactions and I think if we are going to go into this aspect of discussion, we will probably need to be private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that occurred to me. Certainly we'll need to redact portions of this. Dr. Karadzic, although it's preferable to be in public session, I think Mr. Tieger's right. If this line of cross-examination continues in this way, it's probably inevitable that we'll have to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about my participation, my influence, and my role in military matters?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: As regard your participation, your influence, and your role, I had no knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see what other conclusions you drew based on feelings and assumptions. Now, can you please look at page 30 of your amalgamated statement, the last paragraph -- or the penultimate paragraph, rather. Question: "[In English] Did events elsewhere in Bosnia appear to have any effect on events in Sarajevo?" [Interpretation] The answer: "[In English] I had the feeling that when actions would take place in Krajina or the enclaves, the pressure on Sarajevo would go down." [Interpretation] And further on: "[In English] I am not sure." [Interpretation] Was this your answer?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes, this is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we heard evidence from other witnesses based on their feelings and recollections that were contrary, that if there was fighting elsewhere the fighting in Sarajevo intensified as well, but it seems that you are not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you know very well that's improper and inappropriate, and it's no more -- no more than a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, and I withdraw my comment. I withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 2 on page 33. Question: "[In English] Was General Milosevic, for example, aware that these sorts of things were being reported in the media?" [Interpretation] Answer: "[In English] He must have known, but it was just an assumption. He never talked to me about it." [Interpretation] Is this another conclusion which is based on the assumptions? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 22 of your statement, paragraph 4. The Judge asked you with regarding to sniping activities. "[In English] ... The sniping as such and the frequency of sniping was something that was authorised and ordered by the accused?" [Interpretation] Answer: "[In English] In my opinion, yes, indeed, that is correct. As far as the shelling is concerned, when he had artillery means available, yes, but it is possible - and I don't have this kind of information - that reinforcements were given by his superiors to increase the strength of the shelling of the town. But the SRK did have within its means indirect artillery," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] So you had no information about this, but, nevertheless, you made your own conclusions somehow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think that needs to be parsed out. There's a reference to this kind of information within the body of the answer that was quoted, but it's a reference to something particular in there. So if Dr. Karadzic is going to ask the witness about that, he should do so rather than attempt to embrace it or have it encompassed in the -- the earlier answer the witness gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yeah. Can you reformulate your question, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With regard to sniping and shelling, did you have any information and proof, or did you arrive at your conclusions in a different manner?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: With regard to sniping, sniping activities, I indicated in my testimony that we had taken into account all the sniping activities of which we knew where they were coming from. As regards shelling, given what I knew, what we all knew, about the artillery units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, a brief analysis was enough to show that it was possible to intensify the shelling by some artillery equipment assigned to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the sniping and shelling incidents about which you drew conclusions that they had come from the Serbian side, were any proper criminal investigations carried out with respect to these incidents?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Every time there was a sniping incident or shelling, several actions were taken. First of all, UN observers reported about this to the relevant authorities. The UNPROFOR units were tasked to report, analyse, and to define, using military procedures, where the shelling had come from. In these analyses or procedures, they had to analyse the impact, the trajectory of the shells, the verification by experts on how weapons had been used. Once all this had been done, all the information acquired were analysed by experts in various areas, trajectories, artillery equipment. Then they would draft the report, and it's only when there was some level of convergence between all the conclusions that we would indicate what the origin of the sniping or the shelling was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can we get these investigation reports and materials that served as a basis for the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I don't know where those documents were ultimately sent to. They belonged to UNPROFOR. Where are they now? Well, they're most probably in the archives of UNPROFOR. I don't think that those documents were kept by the military personnel. Military personnel do not keep documents, whatever their position or their grade. They do not keep with themselves documents relating to actions, orders, investigations. Everything is sent to the organisation under which that particular person was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if we have to go to private session. This concerns a battalion that was deployed in the city of Sarajevo and that was acting as a source of information. I believe we will have to go into private session for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: (redacted) [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I didn't had in mind the idea that there were straight lines. What I thought was whether there were positions facing one another. Now, could anything enter the Muslim-held territory without flying over the Muslim separation line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: When you say "enter the Muslim-held territory," what -- what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the Muslim-held territory was the area under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the lines of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes. There was an area held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a confrontation line on which UNPROFOR posts were installed, and beyond that line you had areas held by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is P2417 or D2982. Would you kindly look at this article, and can you look at the first part of it, paragraph 3, where it says that this officer said: "[In English] We find it almost impossible to believe, but we are sure that it is true." [Interpretation] Here it has been confirmed to this journalist that the Muslims fired at their own civilians. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] ... media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think there was a substantial gap in the interpretation there, which was very useful in testing my French, but I don't think is otherwise going to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you say now that you don't agree entirely with the conclusions from this article. Can we now go with yes and no answers. I really lose too much time if I put too long questions and you give me answers that are too long. Do you agree with what is being alleged in this article?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I don't have to agree or disagree with an article. You are telling me that I'm providing long answers, but I don't have to answer that I agree with a journalist or that I disagree with journalist. I am not at the same level as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then look at page 43 of your amalgamated statement where you completely agree. You say: "Yes, yes. [In English] Absolutely so. I agree with this analysis." [Interpretation] A little bit lower, towards the end of that page, you say: "[In English] Yes, that is accurate. The statement is accurate."

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Please place it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 43 of the amalgamated statement. 1D2982. Actually, it's P2141; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the accused is certainly entitled to ask whatever questions he may wish arising from information in the article, but as I understand the examination right now, the original question was focused on whether or not the witness agreed with the article. Now he's taken to portions of his statement that are clearly focused on particular information in the article and that is being used to -- allegedly to contradict his assertion with regard to the article in its entirety. So I think a little more focus would be much more fair to the witness and much more illuminating, ultimately, to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that must be right. And bear in mind unless an article in a newspaper is adopted by the witness, the simple fact that it's written in an article is of little moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at what is in this question. It is stated here that it is said in the article that a definite investigation established -- the French marine unit that -- that was patrolling against sniper action, said that they had established that the fire had come from a building that was held by Bosnian soldiers, soldiers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and their security forces. And then here is the question: "[In English] Is that what the results were of the investigation that you were involved in concerning a building somewhere around June 8th?" [Interpretation] The answer is: "[In English] Yes, exactly. [Interpretation] And then it says: "[In English] This is exactly what my soldiers said. When their report reached me I just said, Is this an impression of yours? Are you absolutely concern that the fire originated from the Bosnians, and they answered that it was very likely that it came from their place." [Interpretation] Witness, sir, is it correct that you did not accept their impressions but that you were seeking absolute certainty in their answers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: That is quite correct, and if you read the rest of the statement, I would like to specify that given the way in which the questions were phrased, two incidents had been mixed up, and the statements also specifies that the incident you are currently talking about led to a very fine-tuned analysis and came to the conclusion that this was a real question mark. But as far as another incident was concerned, we were a hundred per cent sure, and this is something which I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Although you assert that the Serbs terrorised the civilian population in Sarajevo by snipers, you say that you didn't have any information about that, and this conclusion of yours boils down to pure speculation, which you did not permit your soldiers, however; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I -- okay. I don't think the witness needs my help. I'll let him answer. But that's extremely -- it's a question that assumes facts not in evidence, it's argument, and -- but I'm sure the witness is capable of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you live in a town where people are being killed and people are being injured and your soldiers likewise, you try to understand how all this has happened, and a succession of facts lead you to believe -- analysis reports also, question marks and questions put to the military lead you to believe that there is a convergence of actions coming into play and that beyond all forms of assumptions one reaches the conclusion that the civilian population is the target of an aggression on the Serb side. I think we have demonstrated our impartiality, and as far as I'm concerned, I didn't think we ever engaged in an unverified conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Mr. Tieger's objection, in my previous question, the witness confirmed that he did not accept impressions from his soldiers but that he asked them to be sure. That was the link in my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, sir, when you say something, do you say that you're absolutely sure of it? Do you state only something that you know for sure, or do you express impressions and beliefs to a large part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, that's an extraordinarily broad question, and I suspect it stems in part from your qualifications in psychiatry, but it's a very difficult question for a witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me then try to rephrase that. Can you state with certainty that Serbs terrorised the citizens of Sarajevo by sniper fire in an organised manner, that this was a plan and this was a planned activity? With certainty.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: I can state it with certainty. However, I cannot say at what level this was all being planned, which is what I said in my statement. I said that such an action launched against Sarajevo, which was not a neutral area in media terms, could not be designed by locals only. Therefore, these acts of terror were well-thought-out and deliberate actions. But as far as the implementation of these actions are concerned, which refers to the facts in this case, I stated what the origin of fire was only when I was sure who the initiator of the fire was. At the conclusion of -- after conclusions had been reached on the basis of the analysis that had been conducted, I would like to repeat, there was a desire to spread terror among the population, that this materialised on the ground, but that we only drew our conclusions on the basis of these actions when we were a hundred per cent sure. In my view, the aggression was much greater on the Serb side than it was on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that topic. Can I please draw your attention to page 45 of your amalgamated statement. It's at the top of the page. You say: "[In English] Although I am not certain, I believe that the snipers did not operate in a random manner. Their operation was perfectly co-ordinated." [Interpretation] But you are not sure, and you believe things in relation to that. You don't have reliable knowledge. "Although I'm not certain" is not in the transcript. "[In English] Although I am not certain, I believe that the snipers did not operate in a random manner."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: When the accused switches from language to language, a lot of the text is not by the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this sentence of yours indicates that you do not have information or knowledge but you have firm beliefs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: This is an internal problem, i.e., the freedom of the sniper to seize an opportunity when the decision is taken by a superior command. In this particular case, the snipers were capable of targeting or shooting at the targets they discovered as part of an overall strategy aiming at the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question, Witness, sir, relates to the fact that you were not sure of that, but you believed it, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Term "certainty" and the term "belief" are not assessment -- assessments which are based on hot air. When an analysis is conducted in a clear fashion, a number of conclusions are drawn, we could not imagine that isolated actions were undertaken. We believe that there was an overall scheme behind this and this is what I mean. In other words, those people implementing these sniping actions were applying on the ground an intention that stemmed from the military authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you don't have proof of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: The sole proof I have is the consequence of a series of shots. Soldiers or the population were either killed or injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to draw your attention to the crisis relating to the demilitarised zone in Igman. You asserted - this is, let's say, on page 58 of your amalgamated statement - that there was a conflict of the two armies in the demilitarised zone on the -- after which the Serbs retaliated against the civilians in the city of Sarajevo. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: The incident you are referring to is an incident which took place on Mount Igman, where soldiers and Serb military personnel had been killed by Bosnians. This is something which I have stated very clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3381, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Witness, sir, do you know who handed the demilitarised zone over to UNPROFOR? Do you agree that in 1993, the Serbs handed over their territory, the territory that they held, to UNPROFOR for UNPROFOR to control?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: That is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at this document now. In your statement, you claim that Serb soldiers who were killed were in the southern part of the demilitarised zone, and the Muslim army was located in the northern part of the demilitarised zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I claim, Witness, sir, that the Serbs were outside of the DMZ, south of the DMZ, and that that was a post of the military medical service, four of whom were women, nurses, and that they -- their throats had been cut when the -- the Muslim army passed through the demilitarised zone, which was under the control of UNPROFOR. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: That is correct, and that is why I gave orders or orders were given to pursue the Muslims, and we launched an operation to try and retrieve them. This is what is written in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the medical personnel, were they subject to the protections of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ182
utterances.text: This is something I have said in my statement. Any medical staff in whatever army is protected by the Geneva Conventions, and that is one of the reasons why we launched this operation to try and retrieve or find these people who had committed this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at this report by the Agence France Presse which describes this event.
